title: Multi-model assessment of nitracline depth and its basin structure
science_question: How deep is the nitracline in three CMIP6 models, how does its depth differ between the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and how far is each model from the WOA23 observed climatology?
query:
Assess the nitracline depth simulated by three CMIP6 models against the WOA23 observed nitrate climatology, globally and by ocean basin.

Data to use:
- CMIP6 historical `no3` from CESM2, GFDL-ESM4 and MPI-ESM1-2-LR, monthly, 1971-01 to 2000-12, each on its own native grid with its own areacello.
- WOA23 nitrate, the all-time-periods annual climatology, objectively analysed, on the 1-degree grid.
- The WOA23 land-sea mask (landsea_01, ocean is value > 1) and basin mask (basinmask_01).

Definition. The nitracline is the depth of the maximum vertical gradient of nitrate concentration, computed across each layer's own boundaries so that an uneven vertical grid is handled correctly. Restrict the search for that maximum to the top 1000 m: below the thermocline the gradient is weak and noisy, and an unrestricted search picks up spurious deep maxima. Load only the top 1000 m of each source.

Order of operations. Form each model's 1971-2000 climatological nitrate profile FIRST, as the day-weighted mean of the 360 monthly fields, and compute the nitracline from that climatological profile. This is the opposite of what a monthly diagnostic would require, and it is forced by the reference: WOA23 nitrate exists only as a single all-period annual climatology at these depths, so a monthly nitracline has no observed counterpart. Computing it from the climatological profile on both sides is what makes the comparison like for like; say so in the answer.

Units. The models report nitrate per unit volume (mol m-3) and WOA23 per unit mass (micromoles per kilogram). No conversion is needed for the nitracline DEPTH, because the depth of a maximum gradient does not move when the profile is scaled; state that this is why the two are compared directly. A conversion IS needed for the concentration cross-sections of figure 2, where the panels must share one colour scale; convert with an explicitly stated density assumption and report what was assumed.

Climatology periods do not match and cannot be made to match: the models cover 1971-2000 while WOA23 nitrate is an all-period composite spanning 1965-2022. State this mismatch as a limitation of the comparison rather than treating the two as contemporaneous.

Everything stays on each source's native grid unless a step says otherwise. CESM2 and MPI-ESM1-2-LR are curvilinear and must never be sliced by latitude and longitude value.

Follow this procedure exactly.

1. Nitracline fields. Compute the nitracline depth field for each of the three models and for WOA23, as defined above.

2. Global mean depth. Report the global area-weighted mean nitracline depth for each of the four sources, in metres to the nearest whole metre, each on its own native ocean grid weighted by its own cell areas. Report each model's difference from WOA23 in metres.

3. Basin means. Report the area-weighted mean nitracline depth for the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans separately, for each of the four sources, in metres to the nearest whole metre, and each model's difference from WOA23 in each basin. Use the WOA23 basin mask carried onto each model's own grid, and state whether marginal seas are folded into their parent ocean, because that choice moves the numbers. Also state that the Southern Ocean and the Arctic Ocean are separate basins in this mask and are not part of the Atlantic, Indian or Pacific numbers.

4. Pattern agreement. Regrid each model's nitracline field conservatively onto the WOA23 1-degree grid. Build ONE comparison mask shared by all three models: cells that are ocean in landsea_01, have a valid WOA23 nitracline, and have a valid regridded nitracline in all three models. On that mask report for each model the area-weighted spatial Pearson correlation with WOA23 to 3 decimal places and the area-weighted RMSE in metres.

5. Summary. State which model reproduces the observed nitracline best, and whether the inter-basin ordering of nitracline depth in each model matches the observed ordering.

Produce two figures.

Figure 1, a 2-by-2 panel of global maps of nitracline depth: the three models and WOA23, all four on one shared colour scale with a sequential colour map, drawn so that deeper is visually heavier. State in the figure that the model panels are regridded to 1 degree for display while all reported numbers come from the native grids.

Figure 2, a 4-panel longitude-depth section of nitrate concentration through the equatorial Pacific, averaged over 2S to 2N, one panel per source in the order WOA23, CESM2, GFDL-ESM4, MPI-ESM1-2-LR. Cover 120E to 80W and the top 1000 m, put depth on the vertical axis increasing downward, and give all four panels one shared colour scale in the same concentration unit. Overlay each panel's own nitracline depth along the section as a line, so the section shows what the depth diagnostic of steps 1 to 4 is actually picking out.

expected_numeric_outputs.definition: global area-weighted mean nitracline depth, each on its own native grid
model global mean nitracline depth minus the WOA23 value
area-weighted mean nitracline depth within each basin, on each source's own grid
model basin mean minus the WOA23 basin mean
area-weighted spatial Pearson correlation with WOA23 on the shared 1-degree mask
area-weighted RMSE against WOA23 on the same mask
whether the model reproduces the observed ordering of nitracline depth across the three basins
the answer should note the shared shallow bias, the Atlantic being worst, which models reproduce the basin ordering, and that the section exposes CESM2's deep eastern-Pacific nitrate deficit

expected_figures.content: nitracline depth for three models and WOA23 on one shared sequential colour scale, models regridded to 1 degree for display only
nitrate concentration averaged over 2S-2N from 120E to 80W in the top 1000 m, one panel per source on a shared colour scale and a common unit, with each source's nitracline overlaid as a line

grading_notes: The order of operations here is the OPPOSITE of a monthly diagnostic: the climatological profile is formed first and the nitracline taken from it. This is forced by WOA23 nitrate existing only as a single all-period annual climatology; computing monthly nitraclines and averaging them would have no observed counterpart to compare against. An answer that silently does it the other way is not comparable with the reference.

The nitracline depth needs NO unit conversion between mol m-3 and micromoles per kilogram: the depth of the maximum gradient is invariant under scaling of the profile. This was verified directly - converting the WOA23 field and recomputing leaves the nitracline depth identical at 100 per cent of the 41029 valid cells. An answer that converts anyway is not wrong, but one that claims the comparison is invalid without conversion is.
The climatology periods genuinely differ: models 1971-2000, WOA23 nitrate 1965-2022. This cannot be fixed and must be stated as a limitation.
The search for the maximum gradient must be limited to the top 1000 m. An unrestricted search finds weak spurious maxima in the deep ocean and produces a quite different global mean.

Basin means must be taken on each source's native grid with the basin mask carried across by nearest cell, not by regridding the fields to 1 degree first. Whether marginal seas are folded in must be stated.

Where the profile is smooth, in the subtropical gyres especially, the depth of the maximum gradient can jump between levels, so a nitracline map is noisier than a temperature-based diagnostic. That roughness is a property of the diagnostic, not an error.

This case depends on a fix made to layer_bounds_like in src/tools/data_loader.py: CESM2 stores its depth coordinate as float32 while the level table is float64, and before the fix any depth-range subset of CESM2 lost its deepest level and every layer-weighted operation failed. Reference numbers were produced after that fix.

WOA23 has 47 levels in the top 1000 m against the models' 19 to 40, so the observed nitracline map is the patchiest of the four: a finer vertical grid gives the maximum gradient more levels to jump between. That roughness is expected and should not be read as observational error.

The equatorial Pacific section of figure 2 is a display product: a longitude-depth section cannot be cut from a curvilinear grid directly, because the index dimensions are not geographic, so the profiles are put on the 1-degree grid before the band is averaged. Every number in steps 2 to 4 still comes from the native grids.

The WOA23 basin mask gives the Southern Ocean and the Arctic Ocean codes of their own, so the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific numbers stop at their boundaries. That choice moves a basin number as much as the marginal seas do, and other partitions draw it differently (OMIP's region mask, or the Atlantic-Arctic / Indo-Pacific split used for overturning), so it must be stated alongside the marginal-sea choice.
